interview_metadata.name: Iris Trujillo
interview_metadata.protocol: American Voices Project (Park et al. 2024, Table 7) - Full 109 questions

transcript.question_text: To start, I would like to begin with a big question: tell me the story of your life. Start from the beginning -- from your childhood, to education, to family and relationships, and to any major life events you may have had.
transcript.response: Well, I was born in Macon, Georgia, in 1951, and I grew up in a small farming community outside Covington. My people were white Southern farm folks, and we did not have much extra, but we always had a garden, a church family, and somebody at the table if they needed feeding. My daddy worked farm land and later did maintenance work, and my mama took in sewing and then worked in a school cafeteria. I finished high school, which was what most girls around me did then, and I married my husband, Frank Trujillo, when I was young. His family had some Spanish and Louisiana roots, which is where the Trujillo name comes from, though our everyday life has always been very Georgia. We raised two children, Paula and Mark, and now we have grandchildren who are about the biggest joy of my life. I worked here and there when the children were older, mostly church office help, cafeteria work, and helping with bookkeeping for a local hardware store, but my main work was family, home, and community. Over the years I learned to stretch a dollar, cook from the garden, put up tomatoes and peaches, and organize church suppers without getting too fussy about it. Retirement for me has not meant sitting still. I volunteer at church and the senior center, help with potlucks, quilting, book club, and senior bowling night, and I try to keep my home peaceful and welcoming.

follow_ups.question: What part of your childhood still feels closest to you now?
follow_ups.response: The garden, more than anything. I can still smell tomato vines and hear my mama calling us in before supper, and I think that is why I still grow roses, beans, tomatoes, and herbs.

follow_ups.question: Who shaped you the most when you were young?
follow_ups.response: My mama shaped me with patience and thrift, and my church ladies shaped me too. They taught me that if you can make biscuits, sit with somebody, or organize a meal, you can help a whole lot.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us that they've reached a crossroads at some points in their life where multiple paths were available, and their choice then made a significant difference in defining who they are. What about you? Was there a moment like that for you, and if so, could you tell me the whole story about that from start to finish?
transcript.response: The biggest crossroads was after my second child started school. I had a chance to work full time doing office work for a small insurance office in town. It would have brought in steady money, and part of me wanted to prove I could do it. But my mother-in-law was getting frail, the children still needed rides and homework help, and Frank was working long days. I decided to take part-time work instead and keep more of my time for family and church. At the time I wondered if I was closing a door, but looking back it made me the kind of person people count on. I became the one who knew who needed a meal, who needed a ride, and who needed help reading a bill or filling out a form.

follow_ups.question: Do you remember how you made that decision day to day?
follow_ups.response: I wrote numbers on a yellow pad at the kitchen table. I added gas, child care, clothes for work, and then I looked at what my family needed from me besides money.

follow_ups.question: Did anyone try to push you one way or the other?
follow_ups.response: Frank said he would back me either way. A friend told me I should take the full-time job, but my mother said, 'You know your house better than anybody.'

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us they made a conscious choice or decision in moments like these, while others say it 'just happened'. What about you?
transcript.response: It was a conscious choice. I did not have fancy words for it then, but I knew I was choosing a slower, family-centered life over a more regular career path.

follow_ups.question: Did you feel settled after choosing?
follow_ups.response: Mostly yes, though I had little moments of wondering. Once I got busy helping at school and church, it felt like the right place for me.

follow_ups.question: Would you choose the same way now?
follow_ups.response: I believe I would. I might have taken a bookkeeping class earlier, but I do not regret being available to my family.

transcript.question_text: Do you think another person or an organization could have lent a helping hand during moments like this?
transcript.response: Affordable child care and more flexible jobs would have helped. Back then, women like me often had to choose between being fully available at home or fitting into a schedule that did not bend.

follow_ups.question: What kind of help would have made the most difference?
follow_ups.response: A part-time job with health benefits and predictable hours would have been wonderful.

follow_ups.question: Did church or neighbors help during that season?
follow_ups.response: Yes, informally. We traded rides, casseroles, and watching children, but it was not the same as having a real system.

transcript.question_text: Moving to present time, tell me more about family who are important to you. Do you have a partner, or children?
transcript.response: I am married to Frank, and we have been married more than fifty years. He is quieter than I am, likes old cars and baseball, and still thinks he can fix anything with the right wrench. We have two grown children. Paula lives over near Conyers and works in a medical office, and Mark is in Alabama with his wife and boys. I talk to Paula several times a week, and Mark usually calls on Sunday evenings. We have four grandchildren, and they are scattered enough that I do not see them every day, but I keep up with them through texts, video calls, and birthdays. Family is not perfect, but we stay connected. I am the one who remembers recipes, photographs, birthdays, and who likes which pie.

follow_ups.question: What do you and Frank do together in an ordinary week?
follow_ups.response: We have coffee early, watch the Braves when they are on, go to church on Sunday, and sometimes ride out for lunch after errands.

follow_ups.question: How do you usually spend time with your grandchildren?
follow_ups.response: When they visit, I cook what they like, let them help in the garden, and tell them stories. With the older ones, it is more texts and video calls now.

transcript.question_text: Are there anyone else in your immediate family whom you have not mentioned? Who are they, and what is your relationship with them like?
transcript.response: I have a younger sister, Carol, in Griffin. We talk every few days, mostly about family, recipes, and doctor appointments.

follow_ups.question: Do you see Carol in person often?
follow_ups.response: About once a month, sometimes more if there is a birthday or somebody needs help.

follow_ups.question: Do you have brothers?
follow_ups.response: No, just Carol and me now. We had cousins close enough to feel like siblings growing up.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anyone else in your life we haven't discussed (like friends or romantic partners). Are there people outside of your family who are important to you?
transcript.response: Yes, I have a small circle that matters a lot. My closest friends are Linda from church, Ruth from the senior center, and Miss Evelyn from book club. We do not need big outings. We meet for coffee, sit together at Bible study, trade books, and check on each other if someone misses bowling night. I like intimate gatherings better than big noisy events.

follow_ups.question: How often do you see those friends?
follow_ups.response: Usually at least twice a week between church, senior center activities, and little porch visits.

follow_ups.question: What do friends tend to come to you for?
follow_ups.response: Budgeting questions, rides, recipes, and organizing meals when someone is sick.

transcript.question_text: Now let's talk about your current neighborhood. Tell me all about the neighborhood and area in which you are living now.
transcript.response: We live in Covington, in the 30016 area, in a settled neighborhood with a mix of older folks, young families, and people who commute toward Atlanta. Our street has modest houses, yards, pine trees, and a few porches where people still wave. It is not as rural as it was when I was young; there is more traffic and more subdivisions. But I know my nearest neighbors by name. I take biscuits or extra tomatoes across the street, and a couple of neighbors keep an eye out when Frank and I are away.

follow_ups.question: Where do you go most often near home?
follow_ups.response: Church, the senior center, the grocery store, the library, and the garden center when I have talked myself into just one more plant.

follow_ups.question: Do neighbors socialize together?
follow_ups.response: A little. Mostly porch talk, checking mail at the same time, and bringing food when someone has surgery or a death in the family.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they feel really safe in their neighborhoods, others not so much. How about for you?
transcript.response: I feel mostly safe, especially in the daytime. At night I lock up carefully, keep the porch light on, and I do not walk alone after dark.

follow_ups.question: Has anything happened nearby that changed how you feel?
follow_ups.response: There have been some car break-ins around the area, so I am more careful about locking the car.

follow_ups.question: Do you rely on neighbors for safety?
follow_ups.response: Yes. We have each other's numbers, and if a strange car sits too long, somebody notices.

transcript.question_text: Living any place has its ups and downs. Tell me about what it's been like for you living here.
transcript.response: The good part is familiarity, church nearby, and enough yard for my garden. The hard part is traffic, higher grocery prices, and seeing open land turn into busy roads.

follow_ups.question: What would you change if you could?
follow_ups.response: I would slow the traffic down and add safer sidewalks for older people.

follow_ups.question: What keeps you there?
follow_ups.response: Our home, our church, my garden, and the people who know us.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about the people who live with you right now, even people who are staying here temporarily.
transcript.response: It is just me and my husband Frank living in the house full time. We have a three-bedroom house, though one room is more sewing and storage than bedroom now. Our children and grandchildren visit, but nobody else lives here. Frank and I split the rhythms of the house in our own old way: I handle most meals, bills, and church scheduling, and he handles repairs, yard equipment, and the heavier lifting.

follow_ups.question: Do you and Frank have set household routines?
follow_ups.response: Yes. Coffee around 7, breakfast light, chores in the morning, and supper usually by 6.

follow_ups.question: Does anyone help around the house?
follow_ups.response: Paula helps with bigger errands sometimes, and a neighbor boy cuts the grass in the hottest months.

transcript.question_text: Is anyone in your household a temporary member, or is everyone a permanent member of the household?
transcript.response: Everyone is permanent. It is just Frank and me.

follow_ups.question: No one staying short term right now?
follow_ups.response: No, not right now.

follow_ups.question: Has that changed recently?
follow_ups.response: No, it has been the two of us for years.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anyone else who stays here from time to time, if there is anyone like that
transcript.response: Grandchildren stay a night now and then, usually during holidays or summer visits.

follow_ups.question: How often does that happen?
follow_ups.response: Maybe a handful of times a year.

follow_ups.question: Where do they sleep?
follow_ups.response: In the spare room or on the pullout sofa.

transcript.question_text: Is there anyone who usually lives here but is away -- traveling, at school, or in a hospital?
transcript.response: No, nobody who usually lives here is away.

follow_ups.question: No college student or relative away temporarily?
follow_ups.response: No, none.

follow_ups.question: No one hospitalized from the household?
follow_ups.response: No, thankfully.

transcript.question_text: Right now, across a typical week, how do your days vary?
transcript.response: Most days start around 6:30 or 7 with coffee, medicine, and a look out at the garden. If the weather is decent, I walk the garden path for 20 minutes and check roses, tomatoes, and bird feeders. Mondays I often do laundry and bills. Tuesdays may be senior center volunteering or book club. Wednesdays I help with church study group or meal planning. Thursday night is often senior bowling, which is more laughing than serious sport. Weekends are church, family calls, cooking, and sometimes watching the Braves or the Saints depending on the season.

follow_ups.question: What time of day are you most active?
follow_ups.response: Morning. By afternoon I slow down, especially in summer heat.

follow_ups.question: Do you keep a strict schedule?
follow_ups.response: No, I keep a list, but I like room to move things around.

transcript.question_text: At what kind of job or jobs do you work, and when do you work?
transcript.response: I do not work for pay now. I am retired and not in the workforce. My work these days is volunteer work at church and the senior center. I help organize potlucks, call older members who need rides, keep sign-up sheets straight, and sometimes help people understand a bill or use their phone. It is flexible, usually a few hours a week, and I can say no if I have a doctor appointment or family visit.

follow_ups.question: How many volunteer hours do you usually do?
follow_ups.response: Maybe six to eight hours in a regular week, more if there is a church supper.

follow_ups.question: Do you think of volunteering as work?
follow_ups.response: Yes and no. It takes effort, but it feels like service more than employment.

transcript.question_text: Do you have other routines or responsibilities that you did not already share?
transcript.response: I handle our household budget, most bill paying, grocery planning, and prescription refills. I also keep a paper calendar on the refrigerator because I trust it more than my phone. I check on a couple of older church ladies by phone, usually on Mondays and Fridays. In season, I preserve tomatoes, peaches, and sometimes fig jam if someone gives me figs.

follow_ups.question: How do you manage the budget?
follow_ups.response: I use a notebook, the bank app, and a folder for paper bills. I like seeing it written down.

follow_ups.question: Who depends on your check-in calls?
follow_ups.response: Miss Evelyn and Mrs. Carter mostly. They live alone and appreciate knowing someone noticed them.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about any recent changes to your daily routine.
transcript.response: I have slowed down a little in the last couple of years. I used to volunteer for every event, and now I pick what I can do without wearing myself out. I also started using video calls more with the grandchildren, and I order some prescriptions online now. Frank and I both plan appointments earlier in the day because afternoon traffic and fatigue get to us.

follow_ups.question: Was there a reason you started slowing down?
follow_ups.response: Some knee stiffness and just plain age. I finally learned that I do not have to chair every committee.

follow_ups.question: Has technology helped your routine?
follow_ups.response: Yes, when it behaves. I can refill prescriptions, see pictures, and video call family.

transcript.question_text: If you have children, tell me about a typical weekday during the school year for your children. What is their daily routine? And what are after school activities your children participate in?
transcript.response: My children are grown now, so I do not have school-age children at home. When Paula and Mark were young, mornings were cereal, packed lunches, and getting them to school on time. After school there was homework at the kitchen table, church youth group on Wednesdays, baseball for Mark, and choir or clubs for Paula. Nowadays I sometimes hear about my grandchildren's school routines, but I am not the one managing them every day.

follow_ups.question: Do you help with grandchildren's school needs?
follow_ups.response: A little, mostly encouragement, birthday money, and sometimes a ride if they are visiting.

follow_ups.question: What did you value in your children's routines?
follow_ups.response: Supper together, homework done, and being respectful to teachers.

transcript.question_text: Some people we've talked to tell us about experiences with law enforcement. How about for you?
transcript.response: My personal experience has been limited. I have had a couple traffic stops over the years and called the sheriff's office once about a suspicious car near the mailboxes. I try to be respectful, and most officers I have dealt with were polite enough. I also know not everybody has the same experience, especially younger Black folks or people who feel watched more closely.

follow_ups.question: Have police ever come to your home?
follow_ups.response: Only once years ago after a minor fender bender report, and it was routine.

follow_ups.question: Do you know local officers personally?
follow_ups.response: A couple through church events or community meetings, but not close friends.

transcript.question_text: What other experiences with law enforcement stand out in your mind?
transcript.response: I remember after a storm, deputies helped direct traffic when a tree was down near our road. That was helpful. I also remember being uneasy watching news stories where encounters turned violent.

follow_ups.question: Do those news stories affect how you think locally?
follow_ups.response: They make me think training and accountability matter everywhere, even in smaller counties.

follow_ups.question: Have you discussed that with others?
follow_ups.response: Yes, quietly with friends at church and with my daughter.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us about experiences of arrest -- of loved ones, family members, friends, or themselves. How about for you?
transcript.response: I have never been arrested, and neither has Frank. I had a cousin who got a DUI many years ago, but that is the closest in my family.

follow_ups.question: Did that affect the family?
follow_ups.response: It embarrassed him and worried his mother, but he got through it and stopped drinking so much.

follow_ups.question: Any close friends with arrest experiences?
follow_ups.response: Not close friends, no.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they vote in every election, some tell us they don't vote at all. How about you?
transcript.response: I vote regularly. I may miss a small runoff now and then, but I try not to. Frank and I usually vote early because it is easier on my knees and we can avoid long lines. I pay attention to local offices too, especially sheriff, school board, and county matters, because those affect daily life.

follow_ups.question: How do you decide who to vote for?
follow_ups.response: I read sample ballots, listen to local talk, and look for steadiness more than showmanship.

follow_ups.question: Do you and Frank vote the same way?
follow_ups.response: Often, but not always. We talk about it, but we do not fuss over it.

transcript.question_text: How would you describe your political views?
transcript.response: I would call myself moderate and practical, with some old-fashioned conservative habits and some compassionate views that do not fit neatly in one box. I believe in personal responsibility, careful spending, and strong families. I also believe older people, children, veterans, and folks who are sick should not be left on their own. I grew up around people who leaned Democratic when it came to working families, then over the years many around me shifted Republican. I have voted for both parties, though in recent years I have felt more independent because politics has gotten so harsh. I care about roads, schools, health care, Social Security, and whether leaders act decent. I do not like name-calling, and I do not trust anyone who acts like the other side is not human.

follow_ups.question: Which issues matter most to you right now?
follow_ups.response: Health care costs, Social Security, grocery prices, local safety, and keeping schools steady.

follow_ups.question: Do you talk politics openly?
follow_ups.response: Only with people I trust. At church I try to keep peace because arguments can take over a room fast.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about any recent changes in your political views.
transcript.response: I have become less loyal to any party label. Years ago I might have said I leaned one way because that was my family or my county, but now I look harder at the person and how they carry themselves. The pandemic, racial tensions, and all the shouting on television made me tired of extremes. I am more willing to say, 'I do not know yet,' and wait before deciding.

follow_ups.question: What made you less party loyal?
follow_ups.response: The anger. It started feeling like people wanted to win more than solve anything.

follow_ups.question: Has anyone influenced that change?
follow_ups.response: My grandchildren, honestly. They ask questions that make me think past what I heard growing up.

transcript.question_text: One topic a lot of people have been talking about recently is race and/or racism and policing. Some tell us issues raised by the Black Lives Matter movement have affected them a lot, some say they've affected them somewhat, others say they haven't affected them at all. How about for you?
transcript.response: They have affected me somewhat. I am an older white Southern woman, so I know I grew up inside customs and assumptions that I did not question enough when I was young. Watching videos of police violence and hearing Black neighbors talk about fear made me pay closer attention. I would not say I became an activist, but I became less willing to dismiss people's pain.

follow_ups.question: Was there a particular moment that stayed with you?
follow_ups.response: The George Floyd video stayed with me. I could not watch all of it, but I could not pretend it was nothing.

follow_ups.question: Did it change any conversations at church?
follow_ups.response: A little. Some people got defensive, but others wanted to listen more carefully.

transcript.question_text: How have you been thinking about the issues Black Lives Matter raises?
transcript.response: I think there are real issues there, even if I do not agree with every slogan or every person speaking under that banner. People should be treated fairly by police, schools, banks, and workplaces. I also think change has to happen locally, with training, accountability, and honest relationships. My faith tells me every person is made by God, and that means I have to listen when someone says they are being treated as less.

follow_ups.question: What parts are hardest for you to talk about?
follow_ups.response: Admitting how much I did not see when I was younger. That is uncomfortable.

follow_ups.question: What kind of local change would you support?
follow_ups.response: Better de-escalation training, community meetings, body cameras, and fair discipline when officers do wrong.

transcript.question_text: How have you been thinking about race in the U.S. recently?
transcript.response: I think we have come a long way in some ways and not nearly far enough in others. In Covington and around Georgia, Black and white families may shop at the same stores and sit in the same waiting rooms, but that does not mean history vanished. I have been thinking about how land, schools, and opportunity passed differently through families. My own family had struggles, but being white meant certain doors were easier to open.

follow_ups.question: Where did you learn to think about it that way?
follow_ups.response: Some from reading, some from church discussions, and some from listening to younger people.

follow_ups.question: Do you think older white Southerners talk about this enough?
follow_ups.response: No, many avoid it because it feels accusing. But listening is not the same as being attacked.

transcript.question_text: How have you responded to the increased focus on race and/or racism and policing? Some people tell us they're aware of the issue but keep their thoughts to themselves, others say they've talked to family and friends, others have joined protests. What about you?
transcript.response: I have mostly talked with family and close friends. I have not joined protests, but I have read more, listened more, and tried not to shut down uncomfortable conversations.

follow_ups.question: Who do you talk with most about it?
follow_ups.response: My daughter Paula and a couple women from church.

follow_ups.question: Have you changed any behavior?
follow_ups.response: I try to be more careful about old sayings or assumptions and to speak up gently when someone says something unfair.

transcript.question_text: What about people you're close to? How have they responded to the increased focus on race and/or racism and policing?
transcript.response: It varies. Frank is quieter and thinks people should respect police, but he also says officers who do wrong should be held accountable. Paula is more outspoken about racial justice. Some church friends are sympathetic, and some think the whole topic is too political. I try to keep the door open without letting talk turn mean.

follow_ups.question: Has this caused tension in your family?
follow_ups.response: Small tension, yes, especially across generations, but not a break.

follow_ups.question: How do you handle disagreement?
follow_ups.response: I ask questions, lower my voice, and sometimes change the subject before supper is ruined.

transcript.question_text: Now we'd like to learn more about your health. First, tell me all about your health.
transcript.response: For 74, I would say I am doing fairly well. I have high blood pressure controlled with medicine, some arthritis in my knees and hands, and I need reading glasses that I am always misplacing. I walk gently most mornings and bowl once a week, but I do not push hard. I see my primary doctor regularly and try to keep up with screenings.

follow_ups.question: What medications do you take regularly?
follow_ups.response: Blood pressure medicine, a cholesterol pill, vitamin D, and occasional acetaminophen for arthritis.

follow_ups.question: What feels most limiting physically?
follow_ups.response: My knees, especially stairs or standing too long in the kitchen.

transcript.question_text: For you, what makes it easy or hard to stay healthy?
transcript.response: It is easier because I like vegetables, gardening, walking, and cooking at home. It is harder because Southern food can get rich, and I do love pecan pie and peach cobbler. Heat makes exercise harder in summer, and some days arthritis makes me choose the rocking chair over the walking path.

follow_ups.question: What healthy habit are you most consistent about?
follow_ups.response: Morning walking and taking my medicine with breakfast.

follow_ups.question: What is hardest to cut back on?
follow_ups.response: Butter, salt, and sweets when I am baking for other people.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anything big that has happened in the past two years related to your health: any medical diagnoses, flare-ups of chronic conditions, broken bones, pain -- anything like that.
transcript.response: Nothing dramatic like a broken bone, thank the Lord. My blood pressure ran high last year, so the doctor adjusted my medicine. I also had a bad arthritis flare in my right knee after doing too much in the garden. Physical therapy exercises helped, and now I use a kneeling bench instead of getting down on the ground.

follow_ups.question: How did the knee flare change your routine?
follow_ups.response: I shortened my walks for a while and asked Frank to carry heavier soil bags.

follow_ups.question: Did you follow through with physical therapy?
follow_ups.response: Yes, I went a few times and still do the leg exercises when I remember.

transcript.question_text: Sometimes, health problems get in the way. They can even affect people's ability to work or care for their children. How about you?
transcript.response: My health gets in the way some, but not terribly. I plan around my knees and energy, and I no longer volunteer for long standing shifts.

follow_ups.question: What tasks do you avoid now?
follow_ups.response: Long ladder work, heavy lifting, and being on my feet in a kitchen for six hours.

follow_ups.question: Do you need daily help?
follow_ups.response: No, not daily. I am still independent.

transcript.question_text: Sometimes, it's not your health problem, but the health of a loved one. Has this been an issue for you?
transcript.response: Yes, Frank has diabetes, and we watch that closely. He also had a heart scare several years back, so I pay attention to his diet and appointments. My sister has had some breathing trouble, and I worry about her too. A lot of my emotional load is keeping track of who has which appointment and whether they are taking care of themselves.

follow_ups.question: What do you do to help Frank manage diabetes?
follow_ups.response: I cook more greens and lean meat, keep sweets smaller, and remind him to check his numbers.

follow_ups.question: Does caregiving wear on you?
follow_ups.response: Sometimes. I do not resent it, but keeping watch can be tiring.

transcript.question_text: Tell me what it has been like trying to get the health care you or your immediate family need. Have you ever had to forgo getting the health care you need?
transcript.response: We are fortunate to have Medicare and supplemental coverage, but health care is still a chore. Appointments can take weeks, and the paperwork is confusing. We have not gone without urgent care, but I have delayed dental work and new glasses because of cost. Prescription prices can surprise you even when you think you are covered.

follow_ups.question: Who helps with medical paperwork?
follow_ups.response: Mostly me. Paula will look over something if I am unsure.

follow_ups.question: Do you trust your doctors?
follow_ups.response: Yes, especially our primary doctor. I trust her more than things I read online.

transcript.question_text: Have you or your immediate family ever used alternative forms of medicine? This might include indigenous, non-western, or informal forms of care.
transcript.response: Nothing formal like that, but I do use home remedies in the old Southern way. Honey and lemon for a cough, ginger tea, heating pads, Epsom salt soaks, and herbs from the garden. I see those as comfort care, not a replacement for the doctor. If something is serious, we go to the clinic.

follow_ups.question: Any remedies you learned from your mother?
follow_ups.response: Warm tea with honey, Vicks on the chest, and soaking sore feet.

follow_ups.question: Do you use supplements?
follow_ups.response: Vitamin D, and sometimes turmeric, but I tell my doctor.

transcript.question_text: During tough times, some people tell us they cope by smoking or drinking. How about for you?
transcript.response: I do not smoke and never really did. I may have a small glass of wine at a family meal or a sip of something at Christmas, but drinking is not my way of coping. When I am stressed, I garden, pray, quilt, bake, or call my sister.

follow_ups.question: Were cigarettes common around you growing up?
follow_ups.response: Yes, very common, but I never liked the smell.

follow_ups.question: What coping habit works fastest?
follow_ups.response: Stepping outside and deadheading roses or pulling a few weeds.

transcript.question_text: Other people say they cope by relying on prescriptions, pain medications, marijuana, or other substances. How about for you and can you describe your most recent experience of using them, if any?
transcript.response: I use prescription medicines as directed, but not to cope emotionally. For pain I use acetaminophen sometimes, and I had a stronger pain pill years ago after dental work but did not like how it made me feel. I do not use marijuana or other drugs. My most recent pain medicine was just taking two acetaminophen after bowling because my knee was talking back.

follow_ups.question: Are you concerned about pain medications?
follow_ups.response: Yes, I am cautious. I have seen people get too dependent.

follow_ups.question: Do you ever skip medication?
follow_ups.response: I try not to. I use a weekly pill box.

transcript.question_text: How are you and your family coping with, or paying for, your health care needs right now?
transcript.response: We use Medicare, a supplemental plan, and careful budgeting. I keep a medical folder with bills, insurance letters, and prescription lists. We compare pharmacy prices when something changes, and I ask about generic medicines. We can manage, but health costs are one reason I keep savings for emergencies.

follow_ups.question: What health cost worries you most?
follow_ups.response: Dental care and anything unexpected like an ambulance or hospital stay.

follow_ups.question: Do your children help financially?
follow_ups.response: No, not regularly. We try to handle our own bills.

transcript.question_text: Some people are excited about medical vaccination, and others, not so much. How about you?
transcript.response: I am generally in favor of vaccines. I get my flu shot and COVID boosters as recommended, though I may ask questions first.

follow_ups.question: Have you ever hesitated about a vaccine?
follow_ups.response: A little with newer boosters, mostly wanting to know timing and side effects.

follow_ups.question: What makes you decide to get one?
follow_ups.response: My doctor's recommendation and wanting to protect Frank and older friends.

transcript.question_text: What are your trusted sources of information about the vaccine?
transcript.response: My primary doctor is first. I also trust the pharmacist we have used for years and information from the CDC if Paula helps me look it up. I do not trust random Facebook posts. If a friend sends me something scary, I usually wait and ask the doctor before believing it.

follow_ups.question: Do you read medical information online yourself?
follow_ups.response: Some, but I prefer official sites and plain-language articles.

follow_ups.question: Do friends ask you about vaccines?
follow_ups.response: Sometimes, especially older church friends. I tell them to call their own doctor.

transcript.question_text: Now we're going to talk a bit more about what life was like for you over the past year. Tell me all about how you have been feeling.
transcript.response: This past year I have felt grateful but also more aware of aging. Some days are peaceful: coffee, birds at the feeder, a good book, Frank humming in the garage. Other days I feel worried about health, money, and the world my grandchildren are growing into. I do not feel hopeless, but I do feel tender sometimes. I have had to accept that I cannot do everything I used to do.

follow_ups.question: When do you feel most content?
follow_ups.response: Early morning on the porch, especially when the garden is watered and the house is quiet.

follow_ups.question: What weighs on you most often?
follow_ups.response: Frank's health, family being spread out, and the feeling that the world is too angry.

transcript.question_text: Tell me a story about a time in the last year when you were in a rough place or struggling emotionally.
transcript.response: Last fall, a close church friend had a stroke, and it shook me. I came home from visiting her and sat in my sewing room with half a quilt square in my lap, just crying. It made me think about how quickly independence can change. Frank found me and did not say much; he just sat beside me. The next day I took soup to her husband, and doing something practical helped me steady myself.

follow_ups.question: What helped you get through that week?
follow_ups.response: Prayer, making food, and talking with Linda from church.

follow_ups.question: Did you tell your family how upset you were?
follow_ups.response: I told Paula. I try not to worry the children too much, but she knew.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they struggle with depression, anxiety, or something else like that. How about for you?
transcript.response: I would not say I have clinical depression, and I have never been diagnosed with anxiety. But I do worry, especially at night, and I have lonely spells. When that happens, I pray, read a little, or write down what needs doing so it stops circling in my head. If it lasted too long, I would talk to my doctor.

follow_ups.question: What do you worry about at night?
follow_ups.response: Medical bills, whether I forgot something, and sometimes just mortality.

follow_ups.question: Have you ever seen a counselor?
follow_ups.response: No, not formally, though I have talked with pastors over the years.

transcript.question_text: How has it been for your family?
transcript.response: Everybody has their own worries. Paula juggles work and grown children, Mark works hard and does not always say when he is stressed, and Frank gets frustrated by health limits.

follow_ups.question: Do family members talk openly about feelings?
follow_ups.response: The women do more than the men. Frank and Mark show worry by getting quiet.

follow_ups.question: How do you support them?
follow_ups.response: I listen, cook, send cards, and try not to lecture unless asked.

transcript.question_text: Some people say that religion or spirituality is important in their lives, for others not so much. How about you?
transcript.response: Faith is very important to me. I identify as Christian, Baptist, and our church has been part of my life for decades. I attend Sunday service most weeks, a small Bible study group, and women's ministry events when I can. My faith is not just beliefs; it is casseroles, prayer chains, hospital visits, and sitting with people when they are grieving. I do not think being Christian means being harsh. To me it means humility, service, forgiveness, and showing up.

follow_ups.question: How often are you at church in a typical week?
follow_ups.response: Usually Sunday morning and one weekday group, sometimes more if there is a meal or planning meeting.

follow_ups.question: What church activities matter most to you?
follow_ups.response: Bible study, senior outreach, and meal support for families in a hard season.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us they use Facebook, Instagram, or other social media to stay connected with the wider world. How about for you? Tell me all about how you use these types of platforms.
transcript.response: I use Facebook mostly. I look at family pictures, church announcements, neighborhood notices, recipes, and gardening groups. I do not post constantly, but I will share a birthday message or a photo of a quilt or flowers. I use my smartphone for texting, email, video calls, and sometimes looking up recipes. I am not on Instagram much, and I never got interested in Twitter.

follow_ups.question: How often do you check Facebook?
follow_ups.response: Once or twice a day, usually morning and evening.

follow_ups.question: What do you avoid online?
follow_ups.response: Political arguments, miracle cures, and anything asking for money too quickly.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they use Facebook or Twitter to get (emotional or financial) support during tough times. What about you?
transcript.response: I do not use social media for financial support. For emotional support, I may post a prayer request in a church group, but mostly I call people directly.

follow_ups.question: Who would you call first in a tough moment?
follow_ups.response: My sister Carol, then Paula or Linda.

follow_ups.question: Have online prayer requests helped?
follow_ups.response: Yes, for feeling less alone, but I still prefer a real voice.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about any recent changes in your level of stress, worry, and your emotional coping strategies.
transcript.response: My worry has gone up some with health costs and aging, but I am better at saying no. I cope with prayer, walking, quilting, gardening, and keeping my calendar less crowded.

follow_ups.question: What have you stopped doing?
follow_ups.response: Chairing every event and agreeing to bake for every single function.

follow_ups.question: What new coping strategy helps?
follow_ups.response: Writing a short list at night so I can sleep.

transcript.question_text: Now we'd like to talk about how you make ends meet and what the monthly budget looks like for you and your family. What were your biggest expenses last month?
transcript.response: Our biggest expenses last month were utilities, groceries, Medicare supplement premiums, prescriptions, car insurance, gas, and property taxes set aside. Food has gotten noticeably higher.

follow_ups.question: What grocery items feel most expensive?
follow_ups.response: Meat, eggs, coffee, and fresh fruit when I do not grow or preserve it.

follow_ups.question: Do you track categories?
follow_ups.response: Yes, in a notebook with rough categories.

transcript.response: Last month we spent around $3,200, which is a little high because of car insurance and a dental bill. A more usual month is closer to $2,700 to $2,900 for utilities, food, insurance, medical costs, church giving, gas, and household supplies.

follow_ups.question: Do you use credit cards for monthly spending?
follow_ups.response: Yes, but I try to pay them off each month.

follow_ups.question: What spending do you cut first?
follow_ups.response: Eating out, gifts, garden extras, and craft supplies.

transcript.response: We own our home. The mortgage is paid off, which is a blessing, but of course we still have taxes, insurance, repairs, and utilities.

follow_ups.question: How long have you lived there?
follow_ups.response: A little over thirty years.

follow_ups.question: Are repairs a financial strain?
follow_ups.response: Sometimes. A roof or HVAC problem can upset the whole budget.

transcript.question_text: Bills can fluctuate over the course of a year. Seasons change, there are holidays and special events, school starts and ends, and so on. Tell me all about how your bills have fluctuated over the past year.
transcript.response: Summer electric bills rise with air conditioning, and winter can bring higher heating costs. Around holidays I spend more on food, postage, gifts, and extra gas for visiting. Spring brings garden supplies and sometimes home repairs after storms.

follow_ups.question: Which season is hardest financially?
follow_ups.response: Summer, because of air conditioning and higher water use in the garden.

follow_ups.question: Do you plan for holidays ahead?
follow_ups.response: Yes, I set aside a little and buy gifts slowly.

transcript.question_text: Tell me all about how you coped with any extra expenses in the past months.
transcript.response: We used savings for the dental bill, cut back on eating out, and postponed buying new porch furniture. I also cooked more from the freezer and pantry.

follow_ups.question: Do you ever ask family for help?
follow_ups.response: Not usually. I would if we truly had to.

follow_ups.question: What pantry meals do you rely on?
follow_ups.response: Beans, cornbread, soup, frozen vegetables, and canned tomatoes.

transcript.question_text: Some people have a savings account, some people save in a different way, and some people say they don't save. How about you?

I put aside money when Social Security and Frank's pension come in, then try not to touch it unless there is a real need.

follow_ups.question: Who taught you to save?
follow_ups.response: My parents. They saved jars, cloth scraps, seeds, and pennies.

follow_ups.question: What makes you dip into savings?
follow_ups.response: Medical costs, car repairs, home repairs, or helping family in a pinch.

transcript.question_text: Some people save for big things, like a home, while others save for a rainy day. How about for you (in the last year)?
transcript.response: At this stage we save mostly for rainy days: health costs, house repairs, car trouble, and maybe helping grandchildren a little. I also keep a hopeful little envelope for travel because I would love to take a gentle Mississippi River cruise someday. But emergency savings comes first.

follow_ups.question: How serious is the river cruise goal?
follow_ups.response: It is a dream more than a plan, but I do look at brochures.

follow_ups.question: Do you save for gifts?
follow_ups.response: Yes, small amounts through the year for birthdays and Christmas.

follow_ups.question: Any car loan?
follow_ups.response: No, our car is older and paid for.

follow_ups.question: Do you worry about credit card debt?
follow_ups.response: Yes, I dislike carrying a balance and avoid it when I can.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about any time during the past year that you haven't had enough money to buy something that you needed or pay a bill that was due.
transcript.response: We have not missed a bill this past year, but there were times I delayed things we needed, like dental work and replacing my glasses. I would not call us desperate, but fixed income means choosing carefully. A surprise bill can make me rearrange the whole month.

follow_ups.question: What did you delay most recently?
follow_ups.response: New glasses. I stretched the old pair longer than I should have.

follow_ups.question: How do you decide what can wait?
follow_ups.response: Anything urgent for health or safety comes first; comfort and appearance wait.

transcript.question_text: What is or was your occupation? In this occupation, what kind of work do you do and what are the most important activities or duties?
transcript.response: I am retired now, but over my life I would describe my occupation as homemaker, part-time office helper, cafeteria worker, and community volunteer. The paid work I did included answering phones, filing papers, simple bookkeeping, taking lunch payments, serving food, and helping keep things organized. At home I managed children, meals, bills, errands, and care for older relatives. In volunteer work, my duties are coordinating sign-up sheets, calling people, arranging food, setting up rooms, and making sure quieter seniors do not get overlooked. I have never had a fancy title, but I know how to make a plan work with limited money and imperfect schedules.

follow_ups.question: Which work felt most meaningful?
follow_ups.response: The volunteer and church work, because I could see people being helped.

follow_ups.question: What skill did paid work teach you?

follow_ups.response: Yes, very much so.

transcript.question_text: What was her job? What kind of work did she do? What were her most important activities or duties?
transcript.response: My mother worked in a school cafeteria and also did sewing for people. In the cafeteria she cooked, served meals, cleaned, and kept children moving through the line. With sewing she altered clothes, hemmed dresses, and patched work pants.

follow_ups.question: Did you learn cooking from her?
follow_ups.response: Yes, especially biscuits, greens, pies, and stretching leftovers.

follow_ups.question: Did you learn sewing from her?
follow_ups.response: Yes, that is where my quilting started.

transcript.question_text: What kind of place did she work for? What kind of business was it? What did they make or do where she worked?
transcript.response: She worked for the public school cafeteria. They prepared breakfast and lunch for students and staff. It was practical, steady work, and the cafeteria ladies were important people in a school even if nobody called them that.

follow_ups.question: Was the workplace close to home?
follow_ups.response: Yes, close enough that people knew her.

follow_ups.question: Did she like it?
follow_ups.response: She liked feeding children, though the work was hard on her feet.

transcript.question_text: Did your dad work for pay for at least a year while you were growing up?
transcript.response: Yes, my dad worked for pay.

follow_ups.question: Did he work steadily?
follow_ups.response: Yes, though farm work changed with seasons.

follow_ups.question: Did he retire from one job?
follow_ups.response: No, he worked different kinds of labor over time.

transcript.question_text: What was his job? What kind of work did he do? What were his most important activities or duties?
transcript.response: My dad farmed and later did maintenance work. On the farm he planted, harvested, repaired equipment, tended animals, and did whatever the season demanded. In maintenance he fixed buildings, handled basic plumbing, repaired machinery, and kept things running.

follow_ups.question: Did you help with farm chores?
follow_ups.response: Yes, we picked, shelled, weeded, and helped preserve food.

follow_ups.question: What did you learn from him?
follow_ups.response: Work ethic, making do, and not wasting what you have.

transcript.question_text: What kind of place did he work for? What kind of business was it? What did they make or do where he worked?
transcript.response: He worked on farms and later for a small local manufacturing and property maintenance outfit. The farm produced crops and kept some livestock. The maintenance work supported buildings and equipment for local businesses.

follow_ups.question: Was his work physically hard?
follow_ups.response: Very hard. He came home tired most days.

follow_ups.question: Was the family income steady?
follow_ups.response: Not always. My parents had to stretch every dollar.

transcript.question_text: We all have hopes about what our future will look like. Imagine yourself a few years from now. Maybe you want your life to be the same in some ways as it is now. Maybe you want it to be different in some ways. What do you hope for?
transcript.response: A few years from now, I hope Frank and I are still in our home, still able to get to church, and still able to sit on the porch together. I hope my health stays good enough for walking, gardening, bowling a little, and cooking for family. I want to finish writing down family recipes and stories so the grandchildren know where they come from. I would love to take that Mississippi River cruise if money and health line up. Mostly I hope for peace: enough money, enough health, family speaking kindly, and a garden that still comes back in spring.

follow_ups.question: What family stories do you most want preserved?
follow_ups.response: Stories about my parents, farm life, church suppers, Frank's family roots, and how certain recipes came down.

follow_ups.question: What would make aging at home possible?
follow_ups.response: Good health care, safer steps, help with heavy yard work, and family nearby enough to check in.

transcript.question_text: What do you value the most in your life?
transcript.response: I value faith, family, health, kindness, and being useful. I value a home where people feel welcome and fed. I value old recipes, gardens, quilts, hymns, and stories because they carry love forward. At my age, I do not need much flash. I want to leave people feeling they mattered.

follow_ups.question: What does being useful mean to you now?
follow_ups.response: Calling someone lonely, bringing food, organizing a ride, or teaching a grandchild a recipe.

follow_ups.question: What do you hope people remember about you?
follow_ups.response: That I was steady, kind, practical, and made room at the table.
